title: Uniform and Ledger
premise: In 1913, Isandro Whitlock drives for Edith Marlowe, a suffragist whose letters he reads and sometimes quietly answers. When the season's floods close the only bridge out of the valley, her movement's funds, messages, and a wounded organizer all become his responsibility to carry alone. As soldiers and magistrates close in on the workshop where the pamphlets are printed, Isandro must choose between the duty that has kept him safe and the woman whose words he has been living by; he finishes the print run as the workshop burns, saves the ledger of names that matters more than money, and crosses the thawing bridge at last — carrying Edith's memory forward after she is arrested in his place.
about_author: Tamsin Thornbury is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing suffrage-era correspondence in northern county records. She writes historical fiction about the people history filed under 'miscellaneous.'

chapters.title: The Weight of Letters
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He drives Edith Marlowe through rain-soaked lanes, reading her correspondence aloud at her request while privately answering the desperate letters himself. Establishes his habit of measuring what can be carried — in a satchel, in a conscience. Emotional beat: quiet devotion disguised as service.

chapters.title: Orders Come Down
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. A magistrate's warning arrives: the workshop printing pamphlets will be raided when the roads reopen. Edith decides to finish the winter's run anyway. Isandro objects; she overrules him with a letter he wasn't meant to read. Emotional beat: love against duty begins its argument.

chapters.title: The Bridge Closes
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Floodwater takes the bridge; the valley is sealed until spring thaw. The courier route dies, the wounded organizer Ruth arrives half-drowned, and Isandro realizes no one is coming to help. Emotional beat: claustrophobia turning into resolve.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Recovering in the loft above the workshop, Ruth catalogs the ledger of names — women who can be trusted, women already taken. She teaches Isandro the cipher hidden in Edith's letters. Emotional beat: grief metabolized into method.

chapters.title: A Winter of Small Treasons
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. He runs supplies across the frozen river by night, lying to the constable who once was his friend. Edith and Isandro share an unspoken understanding neither names. Emotional beat: tenderness sharpened by risk.

chapters.title: The Constable's Ledger
chapters.summary: Constable Hale's POV. Hale discovers a seized letter bearing Edith's cipher and struggles between loyalty to his post and to the boy he watched grow up. He warns Isandro obliquely: they are coming before the thaw. Emotional beat: the price of survival priced in friendship.

chapters.title: Ink Before Morning
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. With days left, the workshop prints around the clock. Edith collapses; Isandro takes the press himself, hands blistered, finishing pages she dictated from bed. Emotional beat: the work becomes the love confession neither speaks.

chapters.title: Smoke on the Water Road
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. Riders come early through the frost. Isandro loads the satchel — ledger, plates, letters — and sets the fire himself rather than let them take the evidence. Ruth escapes downstream; Edith stays to meet the raid. Emotional beat: sacrifice chosen, not suffered.

chapters.title: The Arrest
chapters.summary: Edith's POV. Interrogated in the magistrate's parlor, Edith gives them Isandro's name as her driver and nothing else, taking the conspiracy onto herself. Through the window she watches the river ice begin to crack. Emotional beat: dignity as defiance; farewell without goodbye.

chapters.title: Crossing at Thaw
chapters.summary: Isandro's POV. On the first day the bridge reopens, Isandro walks it carrying one satchel: the ledger of names, bound for London and the movement Edith built. He reads her last letter aloud to the empty road, then answers it, as he always has. Emotional beat: memory carried forward; survival as continuation, not escape.
